title: What Would a Greek Pre-Emptive Strike Against Turkey Mean?
body: A public statement by Greek Chief of Defence General Staff (GEETHA) General Dimitrios Houpis in December 2025 about Greece’s ability to conduct “pre-emptive strategic strikes at great depth” has renewed discussion over the country’s approach to military deterrence. Speaking in a television interview, Houpis said Greece needed the ability to conduct strategic strikes at great depth and that such capabilities could support deterrence through military strength. He also stressed that if Greece ever needed to use such capabilities, the outcome would have to be decisive. The remarks have prompted discussion about what a pre-emptive strike could mean in a hypothetical Greek-Turkish military crisis. A pre-emptive strike generally refers to military action taken when a state assesses that an opposing attack has become imminent. Such a scenario would carry significant military, political and diplomatic risks, particularly because the state striking first could face international scrutiny over whether the threat was genuinely imminent. Phase One: The intelligence red line In the hypothetical scenario outlined by military analysts, a prolonged diplomatic crisis over maritime zones or exploration in the Greek continental shelf reaches a critical point. Turkey could begin moving substantial military forces, while amphibious vessels prepare for operations and drones and ballistic missiles move to a heightened state of readiness at forward bases. Greek intelligence, military surveillance and allied satellite information would then seek to identify signs that the opposing forces had moved from preparation towards an imminent attack. The decisive issue would be the reliability of that intelligence. If Greece acted on incomplete or incorrect information, it could face serious political and diplomatic consequences and potentially be viewed internationally as the party that initiated hostilities. The scenario therefore depends on close coordination between intelligence agencies, military surveillance systems and allied intelligence assets. Phase Two: An immediate attempt to disrupt the opposing forces In the hypothetical scenario, the opening phase would unfold within minutes and rely heavily on surprise. Greek electronic-warfare capabilities could seek to disrupt opposing radars, communications and command-and-control systems. At the same time, Greek fighter aircraft could carry out long-range strikes against selected military targets. The scenario envisages attacks against critical airfields and other military infrastructure intended to limit the opposing side’s ability to launch and coordinate operations. It also envisages Greek anti-ship and precision-guided weapons targeting amphibious forces before they could deploy towards the Aegean. The objective would not simply be to destroy individual weapons systems but to disrupt the opposing military’s ability to coordinate an offensive operation. Phase Three: Defending against retaliation No pre-emptive strike could eliminate an opponent’s entire military capability. The second major element of the scenario would therefore involve dealing with retaliation. Turkey could attempt to respond with surviving missiles, drones and other military assets. This is where Greece’s air-defence and missile-defence capabilities would become critical. The scenario points to the role of modern radar systems, Patriot batteries and the air-defence capabilities of Greece’s new-generation frigates in creating a layered defensive network. The aim would be to detect and intercept incoming missiles and drones while protecting military and civilian infrastructure. Phase Four: Diplomacy after the initial clash The hypothetical scenario envisages the first phase of a conflict ending rapidly rather than developing into a prolonged war of attrition. International actors, including the United States, NATO and the European Union, could then push for an immediate ceasefire and de-escalation. At that stage, military developments would shape the diplomatic environment. However, the outcome of any such confrontation cannot be predicted with certainty. A first strike would not guarantee the destruction of an opposing military capability or prevent further escalation. The wider meaning of active deterrence The significance of Houpis’ remarks lies less in any one hypothetical scenario and more in the broader concept of active deterrence. The idea is that Greece should have the ability to impose a significant cost on an adversary before an attack can produce its intended military results. That approach depends on more than aircraft, missiles or warships. It requires an integrated system involving intelligence, surveillance, secure communications, command networks, long-range weapons, electronic warfare and layered air defence. Greece’s Rafale fighter fleet and upgraded F-16 Viper aircraft form part of this broader capability. Future F-35 aircraft are also expected to add further capabilities in areas such as low observability, intelligence gathering and networked operations. The battle for time In modern warfare, time can prove as important as military equipment. The period between detecting an emerging threat and making a political and military decision may be extremely short. An active-deterrence strategy therefore requires rapid command structures, secure communications, a common operational picture and clearly established response options. Technology can provide decision-makers with information, but it cannot replace the political decision over whether military action should take place. That remains one of the most difficult elements of any strategy involving pre-emptive action. Deterrence and diplomacy remain linked Even in an extreme military crisis, the strategic objective of deterrence remains preventing a wider war. The central idea is to convince a potential adversary that the cost of launching an attack would outweigh any possible military or political gains. If deterrence fails, military capabilities can instead aim to limit the effectiveness of an attack and create conditions for rapid de-escalation. Military strength and diplomacy therefore remain closely connected. The significance of Greece’s evolving defence approach is not simply the acquisition of more aircraft, missiles or warships. It reflects a broader military architecture based on sensors, intelligence, interconnected systems, precision weapons, layered air defence and rapid decision-making. The central question is whether these capabilities can strengthen deterrence by convincing a potential adversary that an attack could fail before it achieves its intended objectives. title: Operation Epic Fury draws at least six U.S. warships from Pacific and up to 5,000 sorties from European bases into Middle East campaign
body: The warships reassigned to the Middle East included the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group and elements of the Japan-based Tripoli Amphibious Ready Group. The Tripoli deployed with the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit, adding amphibious and expeditionary forces to an operation already supported by two carrier strike groups. U.S. Pacific Command also contributed to maritime interdiction, the blockade of Iranian ports and the tracking of ships across the region. The deployment placed Pacific-based naval forces at the center of a conflict far from the theater where they had previously been positioned. Europe carried a broader operational burden, providing bases, airspace access, logistics and strategic lift for forces entering the U.S. Central Command area. Its infrastructure allowed aircraft and personnel to move quickly into the campaign while supporting the flow of weapons, fuel and other supplies. U.S. European Command transferred munitions, equipment, aircraft and personnel while distributing fuel, food and medical supplies. European facilities also stored weapons, maintained combat assets and served as reception and staging points for deploying forces and people leaving the conflict zone. The theater provided more than rear-area support. Forward-deployed fighters, ballistic-missile-defense destroyers, air-defense batteries and counter-drone systems helped protect U.S. forces from attacks originating in the Middle East. Those demands reflected the scale of Operation Epic Fury, which involved more than 50,000 U.S. service members across the Central Command region. At the height of the campaign, the force included more than a dozen fighter squadrons, more than a dozen destroyers and more than a dozen air-defense batteries. Two carrier strike groups maintained continuous coverage during the reporting period, with the USS George H.W. Bush arriving in late April to replace the USS Gerald R. Ford. The handover preserved combat power in the region but required the United States to sustain a large naval presence alongside forces committed elsewhere. The logistics operation was similarly extensive, with U.S. Transportation Command conducting more than 1,500 air missions. At peak activity, 30 to 40 aircraft flew directly into the Central Command region each day, while another 20 to 30 moved through Europe for cargo and personnel transfers. Commercial cargo volumes increased from 9,000 to 74,000 cases a month, equivalent to about 2 million pounds and a 722% rise. Transportation Working Capital Fund obligations connected to the operation reached $2.36 billion by June 30. Iranian missile and drone attacks also forced the U.S. Navy to shift sustainment resources from Bahrain to alternative locations. Diego Garcia provided additional support, but its distance from the operating area extended naval logistics cycles to between 14 and 18 days. The deployment pattern exposed a central challenge for U.S. planners: a large campaign in one region can quickly draw on the ships, aircraft, bases and transport capacity intended to support commitments elsewhere. It also illustrated Europe’s continuing importance to American operations beyond the continent and the trade-offs involved in transferring Pacific forces to a distant conflict. The force movements and operational figures were detailed in the Lead Inspector General report to Congress on Operation Epic Fury, covering the period through June 30, 2026. The report documented the scale of support provided by Europe and the Pacific but did not assess how the transfers affected U.S. readiness or deterrence commitments in either theater.

title: Terror suspects wanted to do ‘big damage’ to air base used by US, Trump says
body: British police on Sunday arrested five men near an air base used by U.S. forces on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offenses after a tip that three vans were heading to the military airfield, which has been used to strike Iran. U.S. President Donald Trump said the suspects had been looking to do “big damage” and had been under investigation by British and U.S. authorities. British counter terrorism detectives leading the investigation said police received a call about three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling towards RAF Fairford in the west of England in the early hours of Sunday. Five men were arrested by armed officers and later held on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. Police said they believed the incident was now contained. POLICE WORKING TO UNDERSTAND CIRCUMSTANCES “We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans said in a statement. “As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident.” Police said a 400-meter cordon was in place around the base as the bomb disposal unit investigated the vans. Local residents in 85 homes in a nearby village were evacuated, and armed officers were patrolling the site. Light Tactical Vehicle drives at the perimeter of the RAF Fairford airbase, Sept. 27, 2026. (Toby Shepheard/Reuters) The British government, which has given authorization to the U.S. to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, said Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being updated on the incident. “I know today’s incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country,” Burnham wrote on X. Britain said in July its armed forces were ​ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned it not to allow U.S. bombers to ‌fly from Fairford, saying any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target. Police have not said who they believed was involved in Sunday’s alleged incident. An Iranian-linked motive is considered the most likely, a source familiar with the investigation said, while a Russian sabotage operation or an Islamist plot are also being looked at. “The arrest in the UK was fantastic,” Trump told reporters, saying it was “an amazing job.” “We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our port and working with the British worked out great. … We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” Trump added. On Sunday morning the base was blocked by armed police while large machinery also prevented access. Reuters witnesses said security had been increased at other bases used by the U.S., with armored vehicles and soldiers at the gates of RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in eastern England. DECLARATION OF A MAJOR INCIDENT “A cordon is in place as a precaution, and the public can expect to see an emergency services presence in the area for some time,” Gloucestershire Police Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone told reporters. The Daily Mail website carried a photograph of five men without shirts who it said had been arrested. A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures. “The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the spokesperson said. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families.” British ministers have also previously briefed providers of critical infrastructure on the threat posed by Russia, with the government increasingly concerned about possible sabotage operations and cyberattacks. Russia denies mounting hybrid attacks on Western nations. A British military air base in central England was broken into in June 2025 by the Palestine Action protest group, which has since been proscribed as a terrorist organization.

title: Russia hits a Kharkiv high-rise overnight, injuring 43 people, then kills four in daylight strikes on central Kyiv and Dnipro
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A Russian strike on an apartment building in Kharkiv injured dozens of people, many of them children, early on 28 September, regional prosecutors reported . Through the rest of the day, Russian drones hit Kyiv, Dnipro, and other cities, killing civilians in several of them. Russia has moved much of its aerial campaign to jet-powered drones that fly too fast for the cheap interceptors Ukraine built against older models. Every switch to a faster weapon reopens gaps in city defenses that Ukraine had only just begun to close. Two floors partly destroyed in a Kharkiv apartment block Russia hit a nine-story building in Kharkiv's Saltivskyi district around 04:00. By early afternoon, the count had risen to 43 injured, including 11 children, prosecutors said . A man of 43 and a girl of 14 remain in hospital with blast wounds, and the others have moderate or light injuries, Kharkiv Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said . Three children lived in the apartment that took the hit. Their father carried them out himself, and none of them was seriously hurt. Rescuers on the destroyed floors of an apartment building hit by Russia in Kharkiv, Ukraine, 28 September 2026. Photo: Kharkiv Oblast Military Administration The strike hit the second floor and destroyed the ceiling between the third and fourth floors. Rescuers brought 32 people out of the building. Across the district, the attack damaged 18 apartment buildings and blew out more than 1,500 windows. More than 100 volunteers are helping city services seal them, Syniehubov added. A resident who fled Kramatorsk a year and a half ago said her family never heard the blast itself. " We didn't hear any explosion. Glass came pouring down, and a column of smoke stood there ," Yuliia Baldzhy told Suspilne Kharkiv. " The children were sleeping in another room, and my husband and I barely squeezed through, grabbed them, and got out. " Yuliia Baldzhy, a resident of the damaged apartment building in the Saltivskyi district of Kharkiv, Ukraine, 28 September 2026. Photo: Suspilne Kharkiv Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said the city had not taken a hit "of this level" in some time. Officials are still establishing the weapon. Syniehubov named guided aerial bombs (KABs) and counted six of them over the oblast in the past day. Prosecutors named a UMPB-5, a Russian munition, as the preliminary version. Terekhov said the city was checking whether it was a KAB or a Banderol , a small cruise missile. Fire among wrecked structures after overnight Russian strikes in Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine, 28 September 2026. Photo: Kharkiv Oblast Military Administration Russia has hit Kharkiv high-rises with guided bombs before. In November 2024, one such strike injured 25 people, including an infant. Explore further Combat shows speed alone can’t catch Russia’s jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers’ assurances. So why can’t they stop them? Kyiv hit through the night and into the day In the middle of the working day, a Russian jet drone struck the main building of the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv's historic center. The attack killed a woman and injured five people, the Kyiv City Military Administration said . Three of them were hospitalized, Klitschko said . People climbed out of windows to escape the fire. Firefighters put out fires at the main building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine and at burning cars after a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, 28 September 2026. Photo: State Emergency Service of Kyiv " Russia will definitely get a response to this, " Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said . Overnight and into the morning, Russian drones hit a gas station in Obolon, a café by a gas station, office buildings, and a 16-story residential building in Podil. The attacks injured three teenagers in Podil, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said . A 17-year-old boy was hospitalized. A firefighter tackles a blaze in a two-story house after a Russian drone attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, 28 September 2026. Photo: State Emergency Service of Kyiv Nationwide, Russia launched 165 drones overnight, 79 of them jet-powered, the Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 112, and hits were recorded at 14 locations. The capital is now under attack daily. On 27 September, Russian strikes injured nine people in Kyiv, and Russia hit a Kyiv data center twice . That evening, a Russian drone struck the Stolychnyi market in Sofiivska Borshchahivka, just outside the city, and killed two people. Zelenskyy wrote that one of the two killed in Kyiv Oblast was a citizen of Azerbaijan. Deaths in Dnipro and Synelnykove Around 11:15, a Russian drone hit a business center in central Dnipro, killing three people. The number of injured rose to 15, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said . Rescuers led 47 people out of the burning building, regional council head Mykola Lukashuk said. " Nearby are residential buildings, a park, a library, offices, shops. The center of Dnipro. In the middle of the working day, hundreds of people are here ," Hanzha wrote . In Synelnykove, a Russian strike on a logistics company's branch killed one person. It injured three others, including a 15-year-old boy now in hospital in serious condition. Overnight, Russian drones also hit infrastructure in the Vasylkivka community and a market in Nikopol. Strikes across other regions In Kharkiv Oblast on 27 September, a Russian FPV drone killed a 67-year-old driver in Shestakove, prosecutors said . A drone on fiber-optic control also killed a 41-year-old woman in a car in Velykyi Burluk and injured a 46-year-old man. Debris at a warehouse after an overnight Russian strike in Odesa Oblast, Ukraine, 28 September 2026. Photo: Odesa Oblast Military Administration Explosions sounded in Poltava overnight. In Rivne Oblast, a Russian attack damaged a detached house without injuring anyone. In Odesa Oblast, Russia struck a warehouse, and an evening attack injured a man of 62 and a woman of 63. Zelenskyy also listed a Palau-flagged ship hit in Odesa Oblast and an ice cream plant damaged in Zhytomyr Oblast, in the same post. title: Ukraine’s disclosure of secret North Korean POW transfer sparks South Korea’s demand for an apology
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Seoul called on Kyiv to explain and apologize for making public the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war, saying Ukraine had broken an agreement to keep the move private and later denied that such an agreement existed, Reuters reported on 27 September. Seoul also said it was reviewing additional measures if necessary. The dispute puts new pressure on ties between Ukraine and South Korea as Seoul supports Kyiv while also dealing with growing military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow. Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said Seoul "expresses strong regret over Ukraine's unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a nondisclosure agreement," according to the Korea Herald. Seoul said Ukraine had requested that the transfer remain confidential, citing fears of a backlash at home for passing up a chance to trade the two soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners held by Russia, though a presidential official called the handover humanitarian, not a prisoner exchange, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported. Seoul went along with the request to protect the soldiers and their families and for diplomatic and security reasons, Seong said, according to the Korea Herald. Ukraine had denied that the two countries had agreed to keep the transfer private. Dmytro Lytvyn, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, replied to a critic on Facebook that "there was no agreement to remain silent" and that hiding the prisoners' destination "would also be wrong," the Korea JoongAng Daily reported . For the 17th or 18th time, Putin promised to take Donetsk “in a few months” – Zelenskyy How the dispute unfolded Zelenskyy announced the transfer on 23 September during a speech at the UN General Assembly. He said Ukraine had recently sent two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. He also described one soldier's attempt to kill himself after realizing he would be captured and accused North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of using his soldiers "like currency," pointing to Pyongyang's improved ballistic missiles and drone capabilities as what it gets in return. The next day, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said the transfer should not have been disclosed and that the two sides had agreed to keep it private. A South Korean presidential official said Ukraine had told Seoul in advance that Zelenskyy might mention the transfer and Seoul had asked that the soldiers' destination not be disclosed, though it was unclear how he would phrase it, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported . North Korean POW reveals he expected training, not fighting against Ukraine Who the two soldiers are The two soldiers—Ri, 26, a reconnaissance sniper, and Baek, 21, a rifleman—were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk Oblast in January 2025, according to their interview with South Korea's Chosun Ilbo. Both had served in North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau and later asked to go to South Korea in media interviews and handwritten letters to defector groups. The two countries' foreign ministers discussed the prisoners' status in March and June, reaching a shared understanding that the case should be resolved under international law and humanitarian principles, according to South Korea's Foreign Ministry. On 8 July, at the NATO summit in Ankara, Lee and Zelenskyy agreed to handle the case on humanitarian grounds while respecting the soldiers' wishes. The two soldiers arrived in South Korea the weekend before Zelenskyy announced their transfer at the UN General Assembly, opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon said . North Korea's role in Russia's war North Korea began sending troops to support Russia's war in late 2024, with initial estimates putting the deployment at more than 10,000 soldiers. Many were sent to Russia's Kursk Oblast. The two countries signed a strategic partnership pact with a mutual defense clause in Pyongyang in June 2024. title: Ukraine outfoxes Russia near Donetsk’s fortress belt with Soviet BTR-60s rebuilt as kamikaze robots, storms a key hub and takes 250 Russian prisoners
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps has defeated Russia at the key settlement of Nove in Donetsk Oblast by pointing it the wrong way. Russia has poured its reserves into counterattacks on a feint axis and "slept through" the real strike, which took the important hub in the village and closed the decisive third season of the Vivaldi offensive, commander Andrii Biletskyi said . Vivaldi is Ukraine's counteroffensive aimed at disrupting Russian forces' plans to encircle the fortress-belt cities in Donetsk Oblast from the north and south. Among them are Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka . These cities have helped hold back Russian forces since 2014. Over its first two "seasons," the 3rd Army Corps and attached units have retaken more than 125 square kilometers , half of it de-occupied outright, and inflicted more than 3,000 casualties on Russian forces. The operation in Nove was its "third season," Biletskyi said, the turning point of the whole operation. The corps liberated Nove, Ridkodub, and Katerynivka and restored control of Karpivka and Novomykhailivka, adding 51 square kilometers to the 176 that had been liberated since the offensive began. Ukrainian forces have taken 250 Russians captive. The feint drew Russia's reserves The victory, by Biletskyi's account, was won by deception. "The enemy was convinced the main direction of the strike was Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna," he revealed, and it burned its reserves counterattacking there. He added that the Russians slept through the real strike, which was concentrated on taking Nove. The village was the prize, a key Russian hub on the bridgehead, ringed by heights that command the surrounding ground. "Who controls the heights holds the initiative," Biletskyi said. By spending its reserves on the wrong axis, he suggested, Russia had little left to hold Nove when the real assault arrived. Old APCs crack the defense To break the strongest fortifications, the corps said, it used a homemade weapon: Soviet BTR-60 armored carriers converted into remote-controlled kamikaze robots, driven into Russia's toughest positions and detonated. In 2024, the Ukrainian forces received another local upgrade of the post-Soviet BTR-60 wheeled armored personnel carrier. This time it was fitted with the BM-7 "Parus" turret, known from the BTR-4 "Bucephalus" The main armament consisted of a 30 mm ZTM-1 automatic cannon paired with a 7.62 mm KT-7.62 universal machine gun. Additional armament might include a set of four anti-tank guided missile launchers mounted on the sides, or two launchers and a 30 mm KBA-117 automatic grenade launcher. As a result, this upgraded BTR-60 saw a significant improvement in firepower, although the vehicle still has very weak armor and less-than-optimal access to the troop compartment. It was the latest of the corps' robotic improvisations in Vivaldi, which have included air-dropped ground drones and Bullspike grenade-launcher-armed UGVs. They are Bulgarian hand-held, rocket-propelled anti-tank grenade launchers based on the Soviet RPG-22, which the Bulgarian defense industry previously produced under license. The corps has leaned on such machines throughout the operation to keep its infantry out of the deadliest fights. Whole units surrender As the defense broke down, Russians gave up in groups, including officers, pilots, and artillery soldiers, the corps said. The 3rd Assault Brigade carried much of the fighting, while the 3rd Border Guard Detachment, named for the fallen Colonel Yevhen Pikus, retook Ridkodub and dug in on the new line, with the 10th Mobile Border Guard Detachment "DOZOR" taking an active part in the assault.
